newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Chirac finds Argentines effusive over French links.
newsitem.headline: Chirac finds Argentines effusive over French links.

text.p: The idol of Argentine tango was born in France and the hero of the nation's independence died there.

More than mere historical footnotes, these are two of a host of elements that helped forge firm commercial, cultural and political ties between France and Argentina that have been highlighted by French President Jacques Chirac's visit.

Chirac, accompanied by businessmen seeking trade and investment opportunities as part of a Latin American tour also including Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay and Bolivia, said on Monday on the first day of a two-day visit he wanted to reinforce "an excellent relationship of confidence, friendship and affection."

Argentine Foreign Minister Guido di Tella rendered homage to "France's contribution to the culture and ideas of Argentina" and the "ancient friendship" that would be revitalised by the French president's visit. Their relations are a source of pride for Argentines who revel in the oft-cited description of their capital Buenos Aires as the "Paris of Latin America."

The architecture and cafes in Buenos Aires betray a French influence. And Argentines, most of whom are of Italian ancestry, like to refer to themselves as "Italians who speak Spanish and think like the French."

While their historic links may be cultural, their current relations are deeply commercial. France is the largest single investor in Argentina since President Carlos Menem implemented economic reforms in 1989 and sold off state firms.

Electricite de France, France Cable et Radio, Lyonnaise des Eaux and Generale des Aux won a big piece of Argentine utilities when they were sold. Other major French players include food group Danone, supermarket chain Carrefour and carmakers Peugeot and Renault.
It perhaps should have come as no surprise that Chirac began his visit by laying a wreath in honour of General Jose San Martin who was a hero of Argentine independence.

San Martin spent his youth in Europe and, influenced by the French Revolution, returned in 1811 to push Spanish troops out of what became Argentina. He returned to France and died there in 1850 after a long self-imposed exile.
Four decades later, Charles Gardes was born in France and would become better known as Carlos Gardel for taking tango out of the Buenos Aires port and making it famous worldwide.

To highlight cultural links between the countries, Chirac has taken on his tour Argentine-born writer Hector Bianciotti, who was recently elected to the French Academy, guardians of the French language.
"France was present in all stages of our national development," historian and political analyst Rosendo Fraga wrote in a newspaper column on Monday.

"The image of France in the Argentine public opinion is very favourable, with eight opinions in favour for every one against," he said, quoting a poll conducted by his firm. "This situation contributes decisively to the broadening of bilateral relations."
